cues.text: I think the most interesting question about Cedric Price would be something about how he still, how is Cedric still a part of architectural culture today, in your mind. That would be a possible question.
and in my view Cedric is a kind of figure that haunts architecture in its contemporary life.
Cedric imagined architecture in the 21st century being something I think fundamentally different
than what it's become. I think his career, his principles, his instinct was to see architecture
as a culture of ideas and almost at times thought experiments about what the world could be and
and that part of architecture's job was to ask questions about the world we know.
I think in that way he haunts architecture and what it's become
because of architecture's increasing and rampant professionalization,
commercial reality, and what I at times call almost industrial condition today.
Architecture is industrializing in at times what I would say are almost horrific ways.
It's getting better at doing more and thinking less.
In other words, architecture is becoming less like Cedric than most of us could have ever imagined.
My immediate impression, which I'll hold on to forever, is that he was an Englishman.
And it had two distinct properties, let's say, for a crude American like me.
like me. One is Cedric's immediate wit and playfulness, which I think people have too
often emphasized as the primary quality of his personality. He was a very witty guy.
On the surface, appeared to be very jokey and playful, but of course what he was doing
with the kind of jokes he would make and the experiments and games that he would play is
really interrogate the habits and the assumptions of architects. It was actually deadly, deadly
serious work, but presented in the most English, low-key English of manners, I think. Incredibly
brilliant kind of critical method. The playfulness was probably the most distinctive property,
but the one is, at least as I got to know the body of work, which to this day I still
think about. The flip side of that, Englishness, is in fact a deeply London sensibility, which
is to see architecture in its global culture and to know exactly where modern architecture
is at any one time in his life. And I don't know where that ability came from, but I think
a huge part of that ability resulted from him being at a place that was deeply connected
to what architecture was doing at all times. London, remember, is an incredibly unique
architectural culture. It's very worldly and has been for decades. One of my absolute favorite
pictures I have of events at the AA, which I've used in lectures around the world forever,
This is a photograph taken in the late 1950s down in what now is our lecture hall,
and what at the time would have been a kind of member space for the association.
And in the middle of the long wall facing the square is an old,
and it looks to me like very grouchy Walter Gropius presenting a lecture
to the crowd of ladies and gentlemen at a series of dinner tables.
And it's a very beautiful picture, and Gropius has got his notes and his reading glasses,
and he's making some pronouncement about what modern architecture is.
And in the foreground of that picture, sitting sort of sideways and looking down at the floor,
is a young Cedric Price, who is the only person in the room not looking at Gropius.
And what Cedric is doing is sort of staring off into space and clearly processing what Gropius is saying,
but in no way following the great master
in a way that every other person in that room is clearly doing.
Cedric is already, and this is only within a couple of years of his graduation,
thinking about architecture in different directions,
and I think it's quite an amazing kind of record of that capacity

Again, I think the primary means for him to be able to do that

It's not unprecedented that some careers have influence because of activities other than building.
Cedric is an extreme example of that.

It's an interesting question many people pose, which is what might possibly be Cedric's relevance to architecture in our time.

I think, for me, one of the most unnerving questions of Cedric's career now is how and why does it live in the way that it does,
